stem: A secure-baseline checklist for workstations asks for the MAC address of the network card. What is analyst-ws's MAC address?
explain: ip link (or ip addr) shows link/ether 52:54:00:a3:7c:19 on eth0. Recording MAC addresses belongs to an asset inventory and a baseline: switch port security, DHCP reservations and network access control all key off it. A MAC address is easy to change, so it identifies a device for convenience, not for security.

stem: One service on analyst-ws accepts connections only from the machine itself, not from the network. Which TCP port is it?
explain: ss -tln shows 127.0.0.1:5432 (postgres): bound to the loopback address, so only local programs can connect. The other TCP listener, 0.0.0.0:22, is open to the network; scanning analyst-ws from outside shows port 22 and not 5432. Binding a service to loopback is a basic hardening step when only local programs need it.

stem: What is this workstation's IPv4 address and prefix length on eth0?

options.why: That is the loopback interface lo, only used inside this machine.
That is the broadcast address (brd) of the network.
That is the link-local IPv6 address, not IPv4.

explain: The inet line under eth0 is the IPv4 address: 10.20.0.50 with a /24 prefix, so the network is 10.20.0.0/24.

stem: Which value is eth0's MAC address?

options.text: ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff
options.why: That is the link-layer broadcast address on the same line, not this card's address.
That is the loopback interface's placeholder address.
That is the IP broadcast address, not a MAC.

explain: The link/ether line gives the card's MAC address; brd is the broadcast address. MAC addresses identify a card on the local network.

stem: Where does this machine send a packet for 8.8.8.8?

options.text: Directly out eth0, to 8.8.8.8 itself with no gateway
options.why: Only addresses in 10.20.0.0/24 are reached directly.

options.text: To 10.20.0.1, the default gateway, out eth0
To 10.20.0.2, the DNS server, which forwards it on
options.why: 10.20.0.2 is not a gateway in this table.

options.text: Nowhere: there is no route to 8.8.8.8 in the table
options.why: The default route covers every address that has no more specific route.

explain: default via 10.20.0.1 is the route of last resort. Anything outside the local network goes to that router.

stem: What does the line '10.20.0.0/24 dev eth0 proto kernel scope link' tell you?

options.text: All traffic for any network must go through the gateway
options.why: Only traffic with no more specific route uses the default gateway.

options.text: The network 10.20.0.0/24 is blocked by the firewall
options.why: A route says where to send packets, not whether they are allowed.

options.text: Hosts in 10.20.0.0/24 are reached directly on eth0
eth0 is down, so the network is unreachable
options.why: eth0 shows state UP in ip addr; this is a normal connected route.

explain: The kernel adds a connected route for the interface's own network. Packets for local hosts are delivered straight to them on that link.

stem: Which of these services can other machines on the network reach?

options.text: PostgreSQL on port 5432, the database server
options.why: It listens on 127.0.0.1, so only this machine can connect.

options.text: Both services, SSH and PostgreSQL, from any host
options.why: Only the one bound to 0.0.0.0 accepts outside connections.

options.text: Neither service can be reached from the network
options.why: Port 22 is bound to every interface.

options.text: SSH on port 22, which listens on 0.0.0.0

explain: The Local Address column shows where a service listens. 0.0.0.0 means all interfaces (reachable from the network); 127.0.0.1 means loopback only.

stem: What does the Local Address 127.0.0.1:5432 mean for the database?

options.text: It accepts connections only from this machine
It accepts connections from any host on the network
options.why: That would be 0.0.0.0:5432.

options.text: It runs as the root user instead of a service account
options.why: The address says nothing about the account.

options.text: It is blocked by the firewall for outside hosts
options.why: Binding to loopback is a service setting, not a firewall rule.

explain: A service bound to the loopback address cannot be reached from the network. It is a simple way to reduce exposure for something only local programs need.

stem: What do the options in ss -tln stand for?

options.text: TCP sockets, in all states, with the timers shown on each
options.why: -l limits the list to listening sockets; timers are -o.

options.text: TCP sockets, listening only, shown as numbers not names
Traffic counters, taken over the last number of minutes
options.why: ss shows sockets, not traffic counters.

options.text: Terminal output, long format, with no header line at the top
options.why: The letters are t for TCP, l for listening and n for numeric.

explain: ss -tln: t = TCP, l = listening, n = numeric ports and addresses. Add -p (with privileges) to see which process owns each socket.

stem: A database is used only by a program on the same machine. Where should it listen to limit exposure?

options.why: That accepts connections on every interface, including from the network.

options.text: The default gateway's address
options.why: A service binds to its own addresses, not to the router's.
That is the broadcast address; a service does not listen there.

explain: Binding to the loopback address is part of hardening: a service nobody remote needs should not be reachable remotely.

stem: What is the state of the connection to 10.20.0.10 port 22, and what is it?

options.text: TIME-WAIT: a closed session that is being held briefly
options.why: TIME-WAIT is the line to port 80, not port 22.

options.text: LISTEN: an SSH server on this workstation waiting for a client
options.why: LISTEN would be a listening socket, and these are connections.

options.text: CLOSED: a failed attempt that never connected to web-03
options.why: ss lists live connections; a failed attempt would not be ESTAB.

options.text: ESTAB: an open SSH session from this workstation to web-03

explain: ESTAB (established) means both sides have an open TCP connection. Port 22 is SSH, and 10.20.0.10 is web-03.

stem: What does the TIME-WAIT line to port 80 show?

options.text: A web connection that just closed and is held briefly by the OS
An active download of a web page that is still running
options.why: An active transfer would be ESTAB.

options.text: A web server listening on this host for new web requests from clients
options.why: Listeners show up with ss -l, and this is a connection to web-03.

options.text: A blocked connection that the firewall refused to allow
options.why: TIME-WAIT is a normal state after a connection closes.

explain: After one side closes, TCP lingers in TIME-WAIT so late packets are not mistaken for a new connection. It is normal and clears by itself.

stem: Who chose the port number 51514 in the first line?

options.text: web-03: it is the port number the server uses for SSH
options.why: The server's side is port 22.

options.text: This workstation: a temporary (ephemeral) client port
The DNS server assigned it when the name resolved
options.why: DNS does not assign ports.

options.text: It is the port registered to the SSH service on web-03
options.why: SSH's well-known port is 22; 51514 is a short-lived client port.

explain: A client opens a connection from a high, temporary port to the server's well-known port. The pair (address and port on each side) identifies the connection.

stem: Which command lists current TCP connections rather than listeners?

options.text: ss -tln
options.why: -l limits the list to listening sockets.

options.text: ip addr
options.why: That shows addresses on the interfaces.

options.text: ss -tn
ping -c 4 web-03
options.why: ping tests reachability; it does not list connections.

explain: Without -l, ss shows sockets that are connected. Together with -l it can show both views of the same machine.
